The point is that they have agreed to a division of labor, that they will follow the chain of command in an emergency, and that they will be accountable for the work.

A good crew still has loyalty. It has trust. It has standards. A captain who is reckless, dishonest, or indifferent to the safety of the ship will lose the crew, and rightly so. But the loyalty of a crew is conditional in a way that the loyalty of a family is not. You can leave a crew. You can refuse to sail with a captain who lies. You can say, “I will not work for this person at this pay under these conditions.” The relationship is serious, but it is not sacred.

The crew metaphor also makes the layoffs harder to mystify. If the company is a crew, then the decision to cut eleven people is a decision about the ship: the route has changed, the cargo is lighter, the weather is worse, the budget is shorter, the work needs to be reorganized. Those are things that can be explained. They can be argued about. They can be wrong. A crew does not ask you to grieve an economic adjustment as if it were a death in the household. It asks you to understand the decision, to judge whether it was well made, and to know what your role will be afterward if you stay.

There is a version of the family metaphor that is not cynical: the idea that companies should treat people with a minimum of tenderness, that layoffs should not be performed with callousness, that people deserve better than a nine-minute script. That is a real value. But the word “family” is too large for it. It tries to carry everything: affection, obligation, hierarchy, forgiveness, permanence, sacrifice. And because it tries to carry everything, it lets the company off the hook for the parts that require precision.

What most companies should say instead is something much less poetic: We are a group of adults working together under conditions that can change. We will try to be fair. We will try to be clear. We will not pretend that a business decision is a blood bond. If we have to cut people, we will tell you why, what it means for you, and what we are doing about it. If we ask you to stay through a hard period, we will tell you what we are asking and what we are offering. If we fail, you can leave, and we will not call your departure a betrayal.

That is not warm. It is not the language of a dinner table. But it respects the actual shape of the relationship, and it gives the people who remain something they can judge. It says: you are not a child here, and you are not a stranger. You are a person with a job, a stake, and a right to know what is happening.

prompt: Make the case that most startups should never raise a Series A. Not as a hot take — I want the actual argument, with the math of dilution and what the money obligates you to do. Around 1200 words, blog post tone.
response:
A Series A is not a growth check. It is a commitment device.

When you raise $10 million to $30 million at a $50 million to $150 million post-money valuation, you are not buying speed. You are buying the right to be judged by a growth curve. The investors are not asking, “Can you make something good?” They are asking, “Can you keep making the same thing bigger?” If your answer is no, you should not raise.

Most startups should not raise a Series A because their real problem is not scale. Their problem is that they have not yet found a durable business. A Series A makes that harder to solve, not easier.

## The math: you pay for a loan you do not need

Suppose you have a small team, a product that is working, and revenue that is growing slowly but meaningfully. You are not dying. You are not even close to dying. You are not being squeezed by a competitor into a corner. You are not out of runway. You are just uncertain.

That is the wrong moment to raise.

Let’s make it concrete. You raise $20 million at a $100 million post-money valuation. New investors get 20%. Your existing holders — founders, employees, angels, maybe a seed investor — are diluted by 20%. If you had a $1 billion exit, your pre-Series A holders would have had a claim on a larger slice. Now they do not.

That is the first cost. It is not dramatic, but it is real.

The second cost is compounding. A Series A usually funds a Series B. A Series B funds a Series C. Each round dilutes again. Each round also raises the bar. The investors who came in at Series A are not only taking a smaller slice later; they are also more likely to demand protective provisions, board seats, consent rights, and a stronger say in what the company does.

The third cost is timing. If you raise early, you price the company before the business has proved itself. If you raise late, after the market turns, you may be forced into a down round or a recapitalization. If you raise in the middle, you may get a good number and a bad obligation. The valuation is not the main issue. The obligation is.

## The money changes the question you are allowed to ask

A seed investor can say, “Find the right customer, the right product, the right wedge.” A Series A investor usually cannot say that without sounding irresponsible. The question becomes: “What is the top of the funnel? What is the bottom of the funnel? What is the multiple? What is the CAC payback? What is the retention curve? Where is the expansion revenue? Which segment is defensible? How do you get to $100 million in annual recurring revenue?”

That question is not wrong. It is just not always the right question.

Some companies need to raise a Series A because the opportunity is genuinely scale-bound. If you are building infrastructure, if you need to build a network, if you need to spend on sales coverage before the market gives you any signal, if you are in a market where the winner takes most, then capital is part of the product. In those cases, a Series A can be rational.

But many startups are not like that. They are service-like, or product-led, or niche, or professional. They have customers who pay because the product is better, cheaper, faster, or easier. They do not need $20 million to learn whether the business works. They need $2 million to find out. They need a sales team, a better onboarding process, a cleaner pricing page, a support system, a partnership channel, a few enterprise references. They need time.

A Series A does not give you time. It gives you a deadline.

## The obligation: growth at the expense of everything else

Once you have raised a Series A, the company is no longer managed for learning. It is managed for the metric that justifies the round.

If you raised on product-led growth, the company becomes obsessed with activation and retention. If you raised on enterprise sales, the company becomes obsessed with pipeline and logos. If you raised on a platform story, the company becomes obsessed with abstraction and ecosystem. If you raised on a market that is not actually there, the company becomes obsessed with pretending the market is bigger than it is.

The problem is not that metrics are bad. The problem is that a Series A makes the metric the identity of the company.

That has several consequences.

First, the company stops exploring. It gets very good at doing the thing that made the round work. It gets worse at discovering what it should actually be doing. A startup that needs to find its real business should be allowed to be clumsy. A Series A company is not.

Second, the company stops being honest with itself. When the growth curve is the company, every bad number becomes an existential threat. A bad quarter is no longer a bad quarter. It is evidence that the thesis was wrong. The founders begin to manage the narrative before they manage the business. They delay bad news. They reframe weak retention as a long sales cycle. They call churn a timing issue. They call low expansion a maturity issue. They call a missing market a category creation issue.

That is not a moral failure. It is a structural one. The capital structure has made truth expensive.

Third, the company starts hiring for the future it promised, not the future it has earned. A $20 million Series A often means 100 employees instead of 30. It means a CMO, a VP of Sales, a head of partnerships, a head of product, a head of data, a head of design, a head of success, a head of revenue operations, and a head of something else that exists only because companies of that size are supposed to have one. It means offices, recruiters, consultants, events, branding, and a board that meets monthly instead of quarterly.

Each of those may be useful. But together they create a fixed cost structure that the business has not yet earned. The company now needs growth not just to succeed, but to justify its own existence.

## The hidden cost: you become a target

A Series A company is easier to buy, easier to outspend, and easier to confuse.

If you have a strong product and a small team, you are hard to attack. You can move fast, change focus, and ignore competitors that are not relevant to your customer. If you have a Series A, you are more visible. You have a press release. You have a job description. You have a brand. You have a board that knows your numbers. You have competitors who now know you exist.

That matters more than founders admit. Many startups die not because they were bad, but because they became legible too early.

A Series A also makes you more vulnerable to the market cycle. In a good market, the obligation is hidden because the metric can be made to work. In a bad market, the obligation surfaces. The company that was “early but real” becomes “early and expensive.” The company that was “small but profitable” becomes “small and underfunded.” The company that was “focused but slow” becomes “focused and irrelevant.”

The money did not create that problem. The money made the problem public.

## What most startups should do instead

Most startups should raise enough to become undeniable, not enough to become expected.

That means raising a small round, or no round, and spending the time finding a customer who would be upset if you disappeared. It means building a business that can survive on the revenue it actually has. It means making the product so good that the growth question becomes a distribution question instead of a survival question. It means saying no to the round that would let you buy a future you have not earned.

This is not romantic. It is arithmetic.

If your product has strong retention, you can often fund growth with revenue. If your customers are concentrated, you can often grow by serving them better. If your market is narrow, you can often become the default in that market before anyone notices. If your unit economics are good, you can often expand slowly and still win. If your team is small, you can often outmaneuver a company with three times your headcount.

A Series A is most useful when the business is already a machine and you need to buy more machines. It is least useful when the business is still a hypothesis and you need to buy confidence.

## The case against

The obvious reply is that startups are supposed to grow fast, and capital is the only way to do it. That is true in some markets and false in many others.

The more important reply is that a Series A does not create optionality. It destroys it. Before the round, you can pivot, shrink, focus, delay, partner, sell, or wait. After the round, you are more likely to accelerate, hire, announce, compete, and explain. The company becomes less able to change because it has already told a story.

That is the deepest cost. A Series A converts a company into a portfolio position. It makes the founders less like owners and more like operators. It makes the investors less like backers and more like creditors of a narrative. It makes the business less like a business and more like a projection.

Most startups should never raise a Series A because most startups do not have a scale problem. They have a clarity problem. And clarity is not bought. It is found, slowly, by doing the unglamorous work of making something real.

prompt: I've run a small B2B SaaS (about $2M ARR, 14 employees) for six years. Everyone tells me pricing is the most underrated lever. I've raised prices twice and both times churn barely moved, which honestly scared me more than if it had spiked. Write a personal essay in my voice about what it means when your customers don't notice a price increase.
response:
For years, I kept waiting for the phone to ring. Not the good kind—the kind where a customer explains, with quiet precision, why they’re leaving. When I raised prices in year two, I braced for it. When I raised them again in year five, I braced again. Both times, churn barely moved. No letters. No calls. A few invoices, the same amount, and life continued.

The first time, I read that as strength. We’d built something people didn’t want to lose. The second time, I couldn’t read it at all.

People tell you pricing is the most underrated lever, and I’ve started to understand why. You spend six years making software, fixing bugs, writing onboarding emails, sitting in meetings where someone says “can we just make this a little easier?” You are trained to respond to friction. You can see friction. You can point to it. You can improve it.

Pricing is not friction. Pricing is a statement. It says what you think the thing is worth. It says what you are willing to stop making for the wrong customer. It says whether you are building for people who need you or for people who tolerate you. And the strange part is that your customers can absorb that statement so easily that you never hear whether you said it well.

That is what scared me.

If I raise the price and someone cancels, I can learn something. They may be price-sensitive. They may be in a category I should not be serving. They may have found a cheaper tool. The churn is noisy, but it is information. If I raise the price and nobody leaves, I have only removed the easiest signal I had. I can no longer tell whether the product is valuable, whether the pricing is correct, or whether the customers are simply too busy, too integrated, or too polite to notice.

A customer who does not notice a price increase is not necessarily a loyal customer. They may be a customer for whom the pain of switching is higher than the pain of overpaying. They may be in a company where the software touches many departments and nobody wants to be the one to start the migration. They may have a budget line that has already been approved. They may be paying for the version of the product they used three years ago, not the one that exists now.

I think about my own customers the way I think about my own habits. There are services I pay for automatically because canceling would take more effort than paying. There are subscriptions I renew without looking at the receipt because the alternative is a small, annoying project. There are tools I keep because the data is there, the team is used to it, and the next person who owns the decision will inherit it. None of that is love. It is inertia.

In a small company, inertia can feel like success. The revenue line holds. The churn number stays flat. The board deck, if you have one, looks calm. But calm is not the same as understanding. I want to know what my customers value. I want to know which part of the product they would miss first. I want to know whether they would stay if the price were twice as high, or whether they would stay only because the migration would be a mess.

The problem is that I cannot ask directly. “If we doubled the price, would you leave?” is a question that produces a socially acceptable answer, not a market answer. “Do you think we are expensive?” is even worse. People will say no, or they will say it carefully, or they will say they understand the value while quietly comparing us to a spreadsheet.

So I have to look for indirect signs.

When I raise a price and nothing happens, I now ask a different set of questions. Who did not raise price? Did the increase apply to new customers only, or to existing ones too? Did I move the line up across the board, or did I create a higher tier that some customers actually wanted? Did I change the scope of what the price buys? Did I make the product better at the same time, or did I simply collect more for the same thing? Did I send a note that explained the change, or did I let the invoice do the talking? Did the increase come with a reason, or with silence?

Silence matters. A price increase without explanation tells the customer that the company has become less willing to speak. It turns a commercial decision into a small act of disrespect. The customer may not cancel, but they remember. They file it under the same drawer as the ignored support ticket, the missed roadmap promise, the feature they asked for that never arrived.

That is why the second raise frightened me more than the first. The first could be explained by ignorance. I was new. I had priced too low because I was afraid. The second could not be explained the same way. By then I had six years of data. I knew which customers complained. I knew which customers recommended us. I knew which customers bought more seats and which customers asked for discounts. I knew enough to make a better decision, and I made a boring one.

I also realized that I had been measuring the wrong thing.

I watched churn because churn is visible. But churn is a lagging indicator. By the time a customer leaves, the relationship has already gone through several quieter failures. They stopped inviting new teammates. They stopped asking for features. They stopped answering my emails. They stopped telling me about the company changes that would have made me more useful. They kept paying because the money left the company without a meeting.

A better metric would have been willingness to invest. Do customers buy more? Do they expand into other departments? Do they recommend us without being asked? Do they fight internally for us when someone proposes a replacement? Do they give us their hard problems, or only their easy ones? A customer who pays the same amount for six years while the company grows around them is not necessarily a healthy customer. They may be a customer whose needs have not changed, or a customer whose internal champion has left, or a customer who has stopped trying to get more value from us.

There is a version of this story where the quiet churn is the real success. Maybe the product is so good that the price increase is irrelevant. Maybe the customers are so aligned that they do not need to be managed. Maybe the market is so small that everyone who needs the tool has already bought it, and the remaining objections are noise. I hope that is true. I cannot prove it.

What I can prove is that I was not thinking about pricing as a decision. I was thinking about it as a number. A number can be raised. A number can be lowered. A number can be tested. But a decision has a point of view. It says what kind of company you are becoming.

If the point of view is “we will keep customers as long as possible,” then a flat churn curve after a price increase is good. It means the customers are sticky. If the point of view is “we will build the best product for the customers who need it most,” then a flat churn curve is a warning. It means you may be keeping customers who do not need the product enough to pay what it should cost.

I think I was afraid of the second thing.

There is a strange comfort in being needed by everyone. It flatters you. It makes the work feel important. It lets you avoid the harder question: what should this product be, and for whom? A company can grow by serving a wide range of customers, each one paying a little, each one requiring a little, each one leaving slowly if the fit is wrong. That can work for years. It can even look like stability. But it can also prevent you from making the product sharp.

The customers who do not notice a price increase are the ones for whom the product has become furniture. They are not angry. They are not delighted. They are occupied. They have built routines around the software. They have trained people on it. They have stored data in it. They have made it part of the company’s normal life. That is valuable, but it is not the same as desire. Desire is what makes a customer tell their peer about you before you ask. Desire is what makes them say, “I don’t know how we did this before.” Desire is what makes them pay more without feeling they have been charged.

I want desire. I do not want only dependence.

So I have started treating pricing as a mirror. Every increase is an experiment in what I believe. If I raise the price for all customers, I am saying the product has become more valuable to everyone. If I raise it only for new customers, I am saying existing customers have earned a legacy rate, which may be true, or may be a way of avoiding the conversation. If I create a higher tier, I am saying the product has different levels of usefulness. If I leave the price unchanged while the product improves, I am saying the market does not yet understand the improvement, or that I do not trust it enough to ask for more.

None of these choices is morally better than the others. But each one has a consequence. A company that keeps raising prices without changing the product teaches customers that the relationship is extraction. A company that never raises prices teaches customers that the product is a commodity. A company that raises prices with clarity and better value teaches customers that the product is alive.

The quietest part of my own story is that I did not know which one I was doing.

I raised the price because I had to. The margins needed it. The salaries needed it. The next round of hiring needed it. I did that to myself, which is not the same as deciding. I made the number do the work of a strategy I had not written. And then I watched the churn number and tried to find reassurance in its stillness.

That is how a founder can be fooled by success. The business keeps paying. The customers keep paying. The complaints remain manageable. The product is not failing. Everything is fine. And because everything is fine, you do not notice that the fine thing is becoming less interesting.

I do not know what I would have done if churn had spiked. Maybe I would have cut the price, which would have told me something. Maybe I would have added value, which would have forced me to think. Maybe I would have talked to the customers who left, which would have been painful and useful. The spike would have been a teacher. The silence was not.

Now I have to make my own teachers.

I will talk to a customer and ask what would make the product obviously worth more. I will ask what they would pay for if we built it. I will ask what they have stopped using, not what they have started using. I will ask what the last purchase of our product felt like inside their company: a decision, a formality, an accident, a favor. I will ask which departments still believe in us and which ones only tolerate us. I will ask what would make them stay if the price were higher, and what would make them leave if the product were slightly worse.

Some of the answers will be false. Some will be evasive. Some will be generous because the customer likes me. Some will be useful because the customer has been forced to defend our product in a meeting and remembers how hard that was. I will sort them. I will not treat one conversation as truth. But I will treat the pattern as information.

I will also watch for the customers who do notice. They may not be the largest accounts. They may not be the ones who stay. They may be the ones who ask for a discount, or who say they are evaluating alternatives, or who suddenly become very specific about what they want. Those customers are telling me where the product is not yet strong enough. They are telling me where the price is doing the work that the product should be doing.

There is a temptation to avoid them. They are inconvenient. They complicate the story. They make you ask whether the product is actually good enough for the people you most want. But a company that only keeps the customers who do not notice anything is a company that has stopped learning.

I think that is the real lesson of the two quiet increases. The first one taught me that I had been too cheap. The second one taught me that I had been too comfortable. The first one showed me that the market would pay more than I had assumed. The second one showed me that the market would not tell me whether I deserved the price.

That is a worse position to be in, because it requires more honesty. You can be wrong about a number and fix it. You can be wrong about value and keep working. But if your customers are silent, you have to decide what you are building without the easy feedback of loss. You have to decide whether you are making something people want, or something they have stopped leaving.

I do not know yet which one we are. I only know that I cannot find out by watching the churn number. I have to make the product say something. I have to make the price say the same thing. And I have to be willing to hear, from the customers who still notice, that we are not saying it clearly enough.

prompt: Essay idea: the weird dignity of businesses that never grow. Like the hardware store in my town that's been the same size since 1974. Is staying small a failure of ambition or something else?
response:
The hardware store has the same fluorescent lights, the same plywood shelving, the same register, and the same owner who answers the phone on the third ring. He has refused every buyout. When a national retailer announced a store in the next county, he did not change his hours. This is not a business. It is a place that happens to sell nails.

The usual account says he is behind. His margins are thin, his inventory is dated, his employee benefits are weak. Measured against a growth company, he is a failure. That measure assumes the purpose of a business is to become larger. It is not. The purpose of a business is to keep a set of people supplied. The hardware store keeps the town supplied with the things that hold it together. It does this in a way a chain cannot: the owner knows which contractor forgets to order washers, which retired mechanic needs the slow‑setting cement, which family is building a shed for the first time.

There is a dignity here that is easily mocked and hard to replace. It is the dignity of a person who has decided that a life is not a ladder. He has made a place that answers to the street rather than to a quarterly report. The store does not need to be famous. It needs to be there on the day a pipe bursts.

This is not a romantic argument for stagnation. A small business that stops improving dies. The owner must still learn new products, price fairly, keep the roof dry, and treat employees like adults. Staying small is not the same as refusing to grow. It is choosing a kind of growth that does not show up on a balance sheet: better judgment, deeper trust, fewer surprises. A company can get better without getting bigger. The hardware store is a test case. If it is still useful after fifty years, its size is not the point. Its point is that it is still useful.

The failure of ambition is only a failure if ambition was the goal. Some people are ambitious in a different direction. They want to be the person the neighborhood can count on. That ambition has its own discipline. It requires saying no to the investor, the expansion, the new market, the brand. It requires accepting that the best day will look like the previous one. For most of us, that is terrifying. For the hardware store owner, it is the whole design.

The strange thing is that the small store often outlasts the large one. Chains close stores when the math stops working. The local shop can survive on a smaller math, because its costs are low and its relationships are thick. It does not need a hundred locations. It needs one block to keep needing it. When the national retailer leaves, the town does not lose a brand. It loses a place that had no alternative.

There is a limit to the praise. A business that never changes can become a nuisance, a monopoly of familiarity, a place where the owner is too proud to fire a bad employee or too tired to try a new supplier. Staying small is not a virtue by itself. It is a virtue when it is paired with care. The store must be good, not merely old. Its dignity comes from service, not from its age.

So is staying small a failure of ambition? Only if you define ambition as expansion. There is another ambition: to make a thing that works for a long time and to be the person responsible for it. The hardware store is not a monument to 1974. It is a daily act. It says that a business can be small, that a person can refuse the obvious path, and that a town is not a market segment. In a culture that treats size as proof of success, that refusal is a kind of seriousness. It is the seriousness of keeping a promise no one asked to be kept.

prompt: Please write an op-ed (roughly 800 words) arguing that the 'customer is always right' principle did more damage to service workers than to customers, and that its decline is overdue.
response:
The customer is not always right. He is often tired, often entitled, and occasionally a small, temporary god, but he is not a permanent truth. The phrase “the customer is always right” sounds like a service principle. It is actually a management trick. It tells employees to absorb conflict that belongs to the system, while telling customers that their experience is a matter of personal entitlement rather than a relationship with a business.

For decades, American retail, restaurants, hotels, and call centers treated customer anger as a kind of weather: something to endure, soothe, and, if necessary, refund. The logic was simple enough to print on a break-room wall. If the customer is upset, the employee’s job is to make the upset go away. If making it go away costs the company a refund, a replacement, or a manager’s time, so be it. Customers pay, after all, and they are the reason the lights are on.

That logic had a surface virtue. It encouraged attentiveness. It pushed companies to notice defects, complaints, and bad experiences. It could produce faster service, more empathy, and a few genuinely good recoveries. But it also quietly relocated the cost of doing business onto the people with the least power in the transaction.

The employee is usually the one who must say the words that make the customer feel heard. The employee is the one who stands in the aisle, the booth, the checkout line, or the phone queue while the customer decides whether this inconvenience is an accident or a personal slight. The employee is the one who must weigh the company’s rules against the customer’s mood, often in seconds, without a clear answer. The customer can leave. The employee usually cannot.

This is where the principle becomes harmful. A restaurant guest who receives the wrong order may be genuinely frustrated. But the person who must apologize, remake the dish, explain the delay, and possibly offer a discount is not the cause of the problem. The problem may be understaffing, a rushed kitchen, a faulty POS system, or a manager who schedules the weekend shift as if it were a math problem. The customer is a victim of the system; the employee is its most visible target.

When companies treat employees as disposable buffers, they learn not to fix the underlying issue. It is cheaper to train a server to apologize than to hire enough cooks. It is cheaper to let a cashier override a return than to improve quality control. It is cheaper to praise “customer obsession” than to admit that the product is unreliable. The employee becomes the place where the company’s failure is converted into a personal inconvenience, and then, ideally, into a saved sale.

The customer is not harmed by being occasionally generous with, but the principle does not create a durable good relationship. It creates a hierarchy in which patience is expected only from the person with the weakest bargaining power. The customer can be rude and still be accommodated. The employee can be reasonable and still be blamed for the customer’s experience. That is not service. That is emotional labor with a loyalty program.

The decline of “the customer is always right” is overdue because the alternative is not to stop caring about customers. It is to care about them honestly. A business should say: here is what we can do, here is what we cannot, here is what we will do to make this right, and here is where the fault lies. If the fault lies with the customer, the business should be able to say so with dignity. If the fault lies with the company, it should fix the process rather than simply soothing the symptom.

This does not mean every customer should be treated as an enemy. It means the company should stop pretending that the customer’s judgment is infallible. A customer can be mistaken about a return policy, a delivery window, or a product’s function. A customer can be angry about a problem that is not the employee’s fault. A customer can demand treatment that no reasonable business should be expected to provide. In all of these cases, the right response is not capitulation. It is clarity.

The strongest service cultures are not the ones that turn employees into apology machines. They are the ones that give employees the tools, the training, and the authority to solve real problems. A good barista can tell you what the machine can and cannot do. A good flight agent can explain what the airline will and will not do. A good store manager can distinguish between a defective product and a customer who simply changed their mind. These are not hostile acts. They are the basic grammar of a fair exchange.

Customers benefit from that grammar too. They may not enjoy hearing “no,” but they benefit when a company’s promises are credible. A hotel that admits a room will not be ready is more trustworthy than one that makes the guest feel like a criminal for noticing the delay. A retailer that explains a return limit is more useful than one that lets a cashier quietly absorb the cost of a policy the company never intended to follow.

The real enemy of good service is not the customer. It is the company that wants the customer’s money but not the customer’s standards. It is the manager who measures success by short-term appeasement rather than long-term reliability. It is the culture that calls an employee “the face” of the brand while refusing to give that face any support.

So let the phrase die. Not because customers are bad, but because the phrase was never about customers. It was about shifting blame. A company that respects its customers will also respect the people who serve them. It will fix what is broken, explain what is possible, and stop asking its workers to pretend that every complaint is a personal moral test. The customer does not need to be always right. The company needs to be right about what it is, what it owes, and where it failed.

prompt: I'm about to quit my job to start a company with my best friend from college and literally everyone I tell makes a face. Can you write something exploring whether starting a business with a close friend is actually as dumb as people think? I want it honest, not reassuring for the sake of it.
response:
The face people make is not a moral judgment. It is a probability estimate. They have seen what happens when a business fails and a friendship survives, and they are trying to tell you that the second part is the part that costs.

The standard advice is to formalize everything: vesting, roles, a buy-sell agreement, a path if one person wants out. This is real, and it is not optional. But it is also a limited protection. A contract can decide who keeps the company. It cannot decide who keeps your friend. The failure it most often prevents is the small, mechanical one: you do the work, your friend does the selling, nobody wrote it down, resentment accrues, someone quits. That is a solvable problem, and the people who are nervous about your plan are not really worried about it.

They are worried about the other one. When a venture fails, the business becomes a record of what each of you did, what you each got, and what you each owe. Those are exactly the questions a friendship has spent years not asking, because the friendship was the easy thing between you. Now the money is the easy thing. You can both be right and still be angry.

There is also a selection effect in the stories you have heard. Failed co-founders who fell out are memorable. Successful ones who stayed friends are less so, because nothing happened. The base rate for any startup is already bad; adding a relationship is not the main risk, it is the amplifier. It does not make the venture much less likely to work. It makes the failure much harder to live with.

So the honest answer is not that it is dumb. It is that it is a different kind of bet. You are not only asking whether this company will succeed. You are asking whether, if it does not, you can still eat dinner with this person. If you can answer that with some confidence, and if you write down the boring stuff before the first argument, then you are not doing something stupid. You are doing something expensive that a lot of people do anyway.

prompt: What's going on psychologically when a meeting runs long because nobody wants to be the one who ends it? Write it up as an essay — I think there's something there about status and politeness in workplaces.
response:
The long meeting is a collective failure of nerve. It is not a scheduling error, not a lack of agenda, not a technical problem. It is a small, repeated act of cowardice, performed by a group of people who have agreed, without agreeing, that no one is allowed to be the one who ends it.

The first reason is status. In most workplaces, the person who closes the meeting is treated as the one who controls it. To end it is to declare, “I have decided this is finished.” That is a claim of authority. If the senior person has not spoken, if the sponsor has not nodded, if the person whose name is on the project has not given the signal, then ending the meeting is a way of stepping into their role. Most people do not want that. They would rather sit in an extra fifteen minutes of silence, or half-listen to someone restate a point, than take a risk that costs them nothing in the moment and could cost them something later.

The second reason is politeness, which in a workplace often means deference. To end a meeting is to impose your judgment on other people’s time. You are saying, “This has been enough for you, even if you have not said so.” That can feel rude, especially if the meeting has included people who spoke only once, or people who seemed to be waiting for their turn. The group keeps going because no one wants to be the person who decides that someone else has not yet had enough. The meeting becomes a way of avoiding a small social cost: the cost of being the one who says no, even when the no is only to another round of discussion.

The third reason is that meetings are not just about information. They are also about reassurance. People stay because leaving can make them look uninvested. If a project is uncertain, if a team is anxious, if a decision has not been fully accepted, then the meeting is a place where everyone can still perform concern. Ending it too soon can feel like closing the door on someone’s worry. The extra time is not wasted time in their minds. It is time in which they are allowed to be serious. So the meeting drags on because it has become a ritual of shared unease, and no one wants to be the one who breaks the ritual.

There is also a simple coordination problem. In a group, everyone can see that the meeting has gone long. Everyone can also see that no one is about to end it. Each person waits for a clearer signal. The manager might end it, but the manager is listening to the data. The data person might end it, but the data person does not want to interrupt the discussion. The junior person might end it, but the junior person does not want to seem pushy. The result is a strange equilibrium: the meeting has passed its useful length, but it has not yet reached the point where someone is willing to bear the cost of stopping it.

This is where the workplace version of politeness becomes most visible. Politeness is supposed to make life easier. It reduces friction. It prevents small conflicts. But in a meeting, politeness can also become a way of distributing responsibility. No one wants to be the one who creates the awkward moment. No one wants to be the one who makes the others feel rushed. So the group keeps moving the awkward moment forward, one silence at a time. The meeting becomes a place where everyone is being considerate, and the consideration is precisely what keeps it going.

The person who finally ends the meeting is often the one with the least to lose, or the one who has been waiting the longest. Sometimes it is the junior person who says, “Should we stop here?” and is rewarded with relief. Sometimes it is the senior person who says, “Let’s take it offline,” and the room exhales. Sometimes it is no one, and the meeting ends only because another meeting is already starting and people leave in a stream. In each case, the ending is not really a decision. It is an escape.

What the long meeting reveals is that workplaces are not only places where work gets done. They are also places where people manage their standing with one another. A meeting is a small arena in which status is negotiated in low stakes. Who speaks first. Who is interrupted. Who summarizes. Who leaves early. Who stays late. Who ends it. These are not trivial details. They are the ways a group learns who has permission to act.

The psychological trick is that ending a meeting feels like a personal risk, even when it is mostly a public service. The person who ends it may be seen as efficient, or as blunt. They may be seen as decisive, or as dismissive. They may be praised, or resented. Because the interpretation is uncertain, the safest course is to wait. The group waits. The clock waits. The work waits.

A better meeting culture would make ending a meeting less like a claim of status and more like a normal part of the process. That means giving the ending a role. The person running the meeting is responsible for stopping it, not for waiting until stopping it feels safe. The agenda should have a time, and the time should be treated as real. The last ten minutes should belong to decisions, not to one more person explaining why a decision is complicated. If someone has not finished, the meeting can say so plainly and continue later. The point is not to make meetings shorter by force. The point is to make the ending a shared function instead of a personal gamble.

The long meeting is embarrassing because everyone knows what is happening. The room is full of people who understand that the useful part is over. They understand that the remaining minutes are a test of who is willing to do the small, unglamorous work of closing things. They sit through it because the cost of ending it is unclear, and the cost of staying is only time. The time is real, of course. But in the moment, it is smaller than the risk of being seen as the one who ended it.

So the meeting goes on because ending it would require someone to take a position. It would require a person to say, with their voice and their body and their seat in the room, that the matter is finished. Most people would rather not. The group learns to live with the extra silence, the extra slide, the extra sentence, the extra nod. It becomes one of the quiet taxes of working with other people: the tax paid by the person who is willing, or forced, to close the door.

prompt: Essay: why apologies that explain are worse than apologies that don't.
response:
# The Apology That Explains

A real apology is a transfer of power. The person who harmed you holds something you do not: the right to say what justifies it. An explanation hands that right back to them.

Consider the difference between two sentences.

"I'm sorry I said that. I was angry and I shouldn't have taken it out on you."
"I'm sorry I said that. I was angry, and when I'm angry I tend to say cruel things, and I'm working on it."

The first is an apology with a footnote. The second is a diagnosis. One says, *I am sorry for this act.* The other says, *I am sorry, and here is the machine that made it.*

## Why the explanation feels worse

It feels worse for at least three reasons.

**It makes the harm optional.** An explanation invites you to weigh it. If the reason is good enough, the apology becomes a form of self-defense that you are asked to accept. You are no longer the person who was hurt; you are the jury.

**It relocates the responsibility.** "I was tired" puts the cause outside the person. The tiredness did the thing. The apology then becomes, *Sorry the tiredness used me*, which is a weaker statement than *I did this and I own it.*

**It can sound like a pre-emptive defense of the next time.** "I was stressed" does not only explain yesterday. It also builds a category: stressed person, unpredictable behavior. The listener hears a forecast.

## But explanations are not always bad

The claim that explaining is always worse is too tidy. Sometimes the harmed person needs the explanation to know what to expect. If someone says, "I'm sorry I snapped; I'm in the middle of a panic attack and I can't always control it," that is not just an excuse. It is information. It changes the relationship from *you are unsafe and I cannot tell why* to *here is a pattern, here is the risk, here is what I am doing.*

The difference is between explaining the act and explaining the person.

An act explanation can be honest: "I said it because I was trying to win, not because you deserved it." A person explanation can become a shield: "I'm just a jealous person." The first leaves room for repair. The second asks you to adjust to a fixed flaw.

## The better order

If you must explain, put the apology first and make the explanation small.

"I'm sorry I canceled. I was scared and I handled it badly."

That is enough. The explanation does not get to expand into a biography. It does not get to list the other person's faults. It does not get to turn into, "Well, you never let me rest, so of course I—"

The test is simple: after the apology, is the focus still on what was done to the other person, or has it moved to the circumstances of the doer? If it has moved, the apology has already begun to explain itself away.

prompt: My grandmother kept every birthday card she ever received, about 60 years' worth, in shoeboxes. When she died none of us knew what to do with them. Write a personal essay about the strange weight of objects that only meant something to one person.
response:
In the living room of my childhood home, stacked against the wall behind the bookshelf, there stood a column of cardboard shoeboxes. My grandmother had received cards from me, from my father, from his colleagues, from friends in cities whose names I could not pronounce. She kept them all. When she died, none of us knew what to do with them.

I have been asked to write about the strange weight of objects that only meant something to one person. I think the word “strange” is doing too much work. The weight is not strange. It is ordinary. What is strange is the assumption that a thing can belong to a person and, at the same time, remain open to everyone else’s understanding.

A birthday card is not a monument. It is a small, disposable proof that a day happened. Someone thought of you. Someone bought something at a counter, wrote on it, put it in an envelope. The card is not the thought. It is the receipt. My grandmother’s shoeboxes are not a record of her inner life so much as a record of the traffic in and around it.

There are two different things we might mean by value. One is the value the card had for her. The other is the value we, the survivors, are expected to find. These rarely agree. For her, a card might have mattered because of the name at the top, the handwriting, the fact that a certain person had sent one at all. For us, the card is a document. We want it to mean something larger than it did. We want it to be evidence of a life, a character, a story. But the card is too small to carry that. It was never supposed to.

This is why inheritance is often a failure of translation. We inherit things, not the minds that chose them. The shoebox is not a portrait. It is a boundary. It says: these things were important enough to keep, and not important enough to send away. That is a strange judgment to make from the outside. We look for the missing logic. Why this one and not that one? Why keep the card from a coworker but discard the letter from a sister? The answer is usually not available. It is buried under decades of small decisions made in kitchens, at desks, in moments of fatigue or tenderness.

I do not think my grandmother’s cards were mysterious. I think they were specific. And specificity is the part of a private life that resists being made public without damage. A card can be read by anyone, but its full meaning depends on a network of absences: the person who wrote it, the year, the occasion, the state of the relationship, the other cards around it. Remove any of those, and the card becomes a generic artifact. It becomes a prop.

There is a temptation, when a person dies, to turn their possessions into a narrative. The boxes on the floor become chapters. The cards become scenes. We want the objects to speak, to confirm or correct the story we have already begun to tell. But objects do not speak in that way. They only repeat. They say, I was here. I was kept. That is not enough to make a life.

What I remember about the boxes is not their contents. I remember their position in the room. They were not displayed. They were stored. They had a place, but not a prominent one. That felt right. My grandmother was not a collector in the way collectors are imagined, with cases and labels and a theory. She was a person who did not throw things away. That is a different habit. It is less heroic. It is also harder to mock, because it is so common. Everyone keeps some things no one else would keep. The difference is degree.

The real problem with the shoeboxes was not that they were full of cards. It was that they forced a choice. Keep them, and they become part of the house, part of the family’s storage, a small permanent claim on space and attention. Throw them away, and we must decide that the days recorded in them are finished. Neither option is comfortable. Keeping feels like a promise. Discarding feels like a verdict.

I think we stayed too long in the middle. We carried the boxes from room to room. We opened them. We closed them. We looked for the cards we had sent, the ones our mother had sent, the ones from people who had died before us. We treated the boxes as if they contained a message that would arrive if we were patient enough. They did not. They contained cards.

There is a particular cruelty in objects that outlast their use. A birthday card is not supposed to be useful after the birthday. Its function is to mark a day, not to survive it. And yet survival is what makes it difficult. If it had been read and discarded, it would have been easier. The card would have been what it was: a moment, passed. The kept card becomes a small accusation against forgetting. It says, this happened, and it was not nothing.

But it was not everything, either. That is the thing we are slow to accept. A person is not the sum of what they kept. A life is not a box. The boxes did not contain my grandmother. They contained a fraction of the paper she allowed to remain. The rest of her was in habits, in voice, in the way she stood in a doorway, in the things she said and then let go. Those things do not come in shoeboxes.

So what should be done with them? I do not know. I know only that they should not be made into a symbol. They should not be described as a whole life. They should not be preserved because they are the last physical trace of a person, as if trace were the same as presence. They should be handled with the same care we would give to a stack of letters we had no right to read: briefly, and with a sense that we are not the intended audience.

If I were to choose, I would keep very few. Not the most elaborate ones, not the ones with the best writing, not the ones from the most important people. I would keep the ones that were difficult to explain to another person. The ones where the meaning depended on something I had witnessed or been told. The ones that would be meaningless to a stranger and therefore, in a small way, still private. I would put them in a single envelope, not a box. A box suggests a collection. An envelope suggests a few things kept because they could not be let go.

The rest I would give to someone who would not feel the need to interpret them. A person who would file them, or burn them, or use them to start a fire, without treating the act as a moral failure. The cards would not need an audience. They had already been received.

What I have been trying to say is this: the weight of a private object comes from the gap between what it meant and what we need it to mean. For my grandmother, a card was a small, dated thing. For us, it becomes a relic, a clue, a burden. We want it to be more than a card. It is not. It is a card, kept for sixty years by a woman who did not throw things away. That is enough. It does not require a story.

prompt: I've noticed that the friends I'm closest to now are not the ones I'd have picked at 22, they're mostly people I kept running into — a coworker, a neighbor, the guy at climbing. it makes me think proximity matters way more than compatibility and that's kind of unromantic? anyway I'd love an essay on that, could go either way on the conclusion
response:
You're right that proximity matters more than compatibility, but only because compatibility is not a property of people. It's an event that happens to people who are in the same place long enough for it to be tested.

At 22 you didn't pick friends by taste any more than you picked a language by taste. You picked the people who were *available*: the cast of your current life, the people your schedule already contained. That cast changed when you moved, got a job, joined a gym. The new people you keep meeting — coworker, neighbor, climbing partner — are the new cast. You're not discovering a flaw in your old judgment. You're noticing that judgment was never the mechanism.

"Compatibility" is a story we tell after friendship, and it's partly true. Two people who get along do share some things: a sense of timing, a tolerance for each other's silences, a similar idea of what a joke is for. But those things are not readable in advance. You can meet someone at 22 who seems perfectly compatible and never get close, because nothing ever asked you to be together. You can meet someone at 30 who seems like the wrong kind of person and become close, because Tuesday evenings kept putting you in the same room. Proximity doesn't replace compatibility. Proximity is what lets compatibility form, or fail, in real time.

The unromantic part is real. It's uncomfortable to learn that the people you love most are partly the people who happened to be there. It flatters less to say "we were meant to meet" than to say "we were in the same building, and neither of us moved." But the romantic version has always been a little false. We don't fall into friendship the way we imagine we fall in love, with a single decisive moment and a person who was waiting. Friendship is closer to weather: it builds from repeated small exposures, and it dies when the exposure stops.

That said, proximity is not the whole story. Plenty of people live near each other for years and never become close. Plenty of coworkers stay at the level of coffee and birthdays. What proximity does is remove the hardest barrier: it makes contact cheap and repeated. It gives you a reason to talk that isn't performance. At the climbing gym you don't have to audition; you just have to hold the rope, or wait your turn, or admit that you're scared of the crux. The coworker sees you in the same unglamorous light you see them in: tired, bad at the software, bad at small talk. That shared exposure is what "compatibility" actually consists of, once you break it down.

So the conclusion could go either way, depending on what you're trying to learn.

If you want a bleak version: your closest friends are mostly a product of logistics, and that means your inner life has less agency than you'd like. You don't choose who becomes essential. You choose which rooms you keep entering, and then the rest happens. That's a little sad, because it means the people you lose are often lost not through betrayal but through address changes, job changes, a gym that closed.

If you want a kinder version: proximity is not a failure of taste. It's the only honest way to meet people. The person at climbing becomes close to you because you have seen each other do the unimpressive parts of being human. That's more reliable than any first impression. The friend you'd have picked at 22 might have been brilliant, but you might never have learned what they were like when a plan fell through, or when they were bored, or when they were wrong about something that mattered to them.

I'd land on the second one, with the first one left on the table. Proximity matters more than compatibility because compatibility is not something you find. It's something that survives contact. The unromantic part is that you can't fast-forward to it. You just have to keep showing up where people are, and let the repeated small moments do the choosing.

prompt: Why 'communication is the key to every relationship' is overrated advice. I suspect some couples are happier precisely because they don't process everything out loud. Argue it, ~1000 words.
response:
The advice that "communication is the key to every relationship" has become a piece of furniture in modern emotional life. It is always in the room, always being leaned on, rarely being used. It sounds wise because it is so vague. It sounds necessary because most relationships do fail from some kind of silence. But the slogan hides a specific assumption: that a relationship is a project in which two people manage a shared problem, and that management requires constant, explicit, verbal processing. If you accept that assumption, the slogan is right. But many of the most stable couples do not run their lives that way, and they are often happier for it.

Most of the advice around communication comes from a particular kind of marriage. The couple is stressed, probably by work, money, children, or a sense that life is passing them by. Their problems are external and recurring: who does the dishes, how to talk to the kids, how to save for a house, how to handle in-laws. For that couple, communication does a lot of real work. It turns private irritation into a joint task. It stops resentment from building in the background. A conversation about the dishwasher is not really about the dishwasher. It is a way of saying, “I am not okay with this, and I need us to be on the same side.” In that context, the advice is not merely true; it is practical.

But the slogan then gets generalized into a rule for all relationships, and that is where it starts to misfire. It turns talk into a duty. It makes silence suspicious. It implies that if a couple is not talking about everything, something is wrong. A man can feel he must explain why he sat quietly on the porch. A woman can feel she must process her afternoon at work into a narrative before her partner is allowed to ask how it was. The conversation becomes a performance of emotional labor, and the relationship becomes a meeting that never ends.

The problem is not that these people are bad communicators. The problem is that the slogan treats communication as the highest form of intimacy. But intimacy is not a transcript. Sometimes it is a shared absence of words. A couple walking home without talking, lying side by side watching a bad film, knowing what to do at breakfast without saying it—these are not failures of communication. They are communication in a different register. They say, “You are not a stranger here. You do not have to justify your presence.” That kind of comfort is hard to manufacture with more talk. If a couple has to keep explaining why they are together, why they are tired, why they are not angry, why the silence is okay, the silence has already become a problem.

There is a difference between processing and narrating. Processing is how you make sense of something that has happened to you. Narrating is how you turn your inner life into a story for someone else to receive. Processing can be private: a walk, a journal, a long shower, a period of not thinking about anything. Narrating can be valuable, but it is not always the first move. If every feeling must become a conversation before it is allowed to settle, the relationship becomes a place where nothing is finished. The partner becomes a therapist, a witness, a co-investigator. That can be wonderful when it is wanted, but it is exhausting when it is assumed.

The happiest couples I have watched tend to have a kind of selective permeability. They do not share everything. They do not need to. One partner may have a thought so private it is not meant to be explained. Another may have a mood that is hers alone for the afternoon. They can sit in the same house without the house becoming a courtroom. They can disagree and let the disagreement cool without a debriefing. They can say, “I am not going to talk about that right now,” and mean it without the relationship collapsing. That is not repression. It is trust. It is the knowledge that the other person is not going to treat your silence as evidence of betrayal.

This is why the slogan is overrated. It mistakes a useful tool for the whole building. Communication can save a marriage. It can also flatten one. A couple that talks constantly may still be lonely. They may be good at explaining and bad at being with each other. They may have a shared language but no shared life. They may know all the words and not the person. The opposite is also true: a couple that says little may be deeply connected, but only if the silence is chosen, not defensive. Quiet can be peace, or it can be avoidance. The slogan cannot tell the difference, so it defaults to talk.

The real skill is not “communicate more.” The real skill is knowing what a silence is for. If a silence is fear, then talk may be needed. If a silence is shame, then talk may be needed, but gently, because shame wants to hide. If a silence is irritation, then talk may be needed before it becomes contempt. But if a silence is rest, then talk may be the intrusion. If a silence is the space in which two people exist without having to perform their feelings, then the couple who breaks it to “check in” may be damaging something.

This is especially true in long relationships. Early on, couples often talk a lot because they are still figuring out each other. They are negotiating the rules: what can be said, what is funny, what hurts, what is private, what is shared. Later, if the relationship is healthy, some of that work is done. The couple has a common ground. They do not need to report every experience to keep the ground from eroding. A long marriage can become a kind of shared habit of being together, and habit is not the enemy of love. It can be one of its forms.

There is also a social pressure behind the slogan that is worth naming. Modern relationships are expected to be self-renewing. The couple is supposed to be each other’s emotional infrastructure. If you are unhappy, you are supposed to talk it out. If you do not talk it out, you are supposed to suspect avoidance. This puts a lot on the relationship. It makes the partner responsible for your inner weather. Sometimes that is fair. Sometimes it is a way of refusing to let a person be a person. A spouse is not an extension of your nervous system. A friend is not a tool for making you feel less opaque to yourself.

The best answer to “communication is the key” is not “communication is overrated.” The better answer is: communication is a key, but not the only door. Some rooms in a marriage are entered through words. Some are entered through action. Some are entered by not doing anything at all, by leaving a cup on the table, by not asking, by letting the other person come back to you when she is ready. A relationship that only has one mode of entry is brittle. If everything must be spoken, then every unspoken thing becomes a threat. If every feeling must be processed, then the feeling never gets to be just a feeling.

So yes, some couples are happier precisely because they do not process everything out loud. Not because they are better, but because they understand something the slogan does not: that intimacy is not a conversation. It is a way of being near another person without turning everything into a case to be made. The couple that can be quiet together, and means it, has already solved a harder problem than the couple that can only say it.

prompt: I'm 34 and I've realized I don't really know how to make friends as an adult without a structure like school or a job forcing it. write an essay about why adult friendship is so hard to start, ideally something that doesn't end with 'just join a club'
response:
# The Architecture of Adult Friendship

When I was twelve, I did not have to know how to make friends. I only had to be in the room. The school building did the work for me: it sorted children into corridors, classrooms, lunch lines, and playgrounds, and then it kept returning them to the same people every day. Friendship was not a skill I had to acquire; it was a residue of repetition. If a kid sat next to me at breakfast, ate lunch with me, got stuck behind me in the hall, and shared a game in the afternoon, then by the end of the week we had something. It might be thin, or mean, or accidental, but it was a beginning.

Most of my friendships did not start with a decision. They started with proximity.

That is why adult friendship is so hard. Adults are not usually placed in the same room every day with a rotating group of strangers and told to talk. Work, at least in many modern jobs, is structured to keep people separated. We sit at desks, wear headsets, use chat apps, attend meetings with the same small circle, and leave before the day has produced much common life. The people we see most are not necessarily the people we could become close to. Coworkers can become friends, of course, but the conditions are often against it: hierarchy, gossip, evaluation, and the fact that one of you might be fired or promoted or quit. Work gives you contact, but contact is not intimacy.

Home is the other structure, and it is even worse for new friendship. It is private. The people who live near you are mostly invisible. You see them through car windows, in driveways, at the mailbox. You may know that someone is alive, that they have a dog, that they have a new fence, but you do not know whether they are lonely, whether they like bad movies, whether they would walk to your house if you invited them. Adult life has replaced the schoolyard with a series of sealed rooms.

There is a second problem: adult friendship often begins at the point where childhood friendship ends. A child can say, “You look sad,” and mean nothing more than that. An adult has to decide how much of a stranger’s life he is allowed to touch. A new acquaintance is not only a person; he is a situation. Every conversation has to be judged. Can I ask about his divorce? Can I be honest that I am bad at making friends? Can I invite him over, or will that make it odd? The more an adult friendship depends on choice, the more it requires a kind of social risk that children never have to take.

A child can be rejected and still see the same kid tomorrow. An adult can be rejected and lose the only avenue to that person. If you invite someone and they do not come, or if you text and they answer days later, you are not merely disappointed; you are recalibrating. You are learning whether this person wants you. That is a small humiliation, and it happens often. Adults do not lack desire for friendship. They lack safe, low-stakes ways of testing it.

The third reason is that adult friendship requires a new kind of time. Childhood friendship can be intense and continuous. You are together from eight to three, with meals and errands and boredom in between. Adult friendship has to be scheduled. “We should hang out” is not a plan; it is a wish. Two adults may both want to see each other and still fail to meet because their evenings are filled with obligations, because one of them is tired, because neither wants to be the one to propose the third attempt. The friendship does not fail because the people dislike each other. It fails because the logistics are too expensive.

This is where the usual advice gets annoying. “Join a club.” “Take a class.” “Volunteer.” “Go to the park.” These suggestions are not stupid. They work sometimes. But they miss the real difficulty. The difficulty is not that adults do not know where other adults are. It is that most adult institutions are organized around an activity, not around friendship. A running group is for running. A book club is for reading. A volunteer shift is for the task. Friendship is supposed to happen around the edges, but the edges are thin. If the activity is the point, the friendship is secondary, and secondary things tend to fade.

A church, a gym, a hobby group, a parent group, a co-op, a sports league: these can produce friends. But they produce them unevenly. Some people are good at staying after the activity. Some people are not. Some groups are full of people who want friends and have the bandwidth to make them. Others are full of people who want the activity, the status, the exercise, the children, the escape, and who would prefer not to become emotionally available to strangers. Joining a club gives you more contact, but it does not remove the awkwardness of contact. It only multiplies it.

The deeper issue is that adult friendship asks two people to create a structure that did not exist before. In childhood, the structure was the school. In adult friendship, the structure is the relationship itself. You have to invent the rhythm. Who initiates? How often? What does a normal meeting look like? Can you see each other for coffee, or only for a full dinner? Can you go for a walk, or is that too casual? Can you invite a partner, a spouse, a child? Can you talk about work, or is that the only thing you have? These questions sound small, but they are the architecture. Without them, the friendship remains a set of isolated events: one dinner, one movie, one walk, one canceled plan. It never becomes a world.

That is why adult friendship often feels less like friendship and more like a project. A project requires maintenance. It requires someone to remember it, to propose it, to accept the awkwardness of starting it again. If both people are tired, the project collapses. If one person is enthusiastic and the other is merely polite, the enthusiastic person learns not to bother. If both are capable but too busy, the project is postponed until it is dead.

There is also a cultural problem. We talk as if friendship is simple, warm, and natural. We use the word as if it were a state of being: “We’re friends.” But adult friendship is often a practice. It is a repeated act of showing up. The people who seem to have many friends are not always more likable, though likability helps. They are often more consistent. They send the message. They make the plan. They accept the second invitation. They do not wait for the relationship to become easy before they treat it as real.

This is not a moral failure. It is a survival strategy. Many people have been rejected enough times to stop proposing. Many people have learned that enthusiasm is mistaken for neediness, or that making plans is annoying, or that other people’s schedules matter more than their own. So they retreat into the friendships that already work: the old friend from college, the coworker, the neighbor who happens to be easy. New friendship becomes a risk without a reward. The reward is a friend, but the friend may not materialize. The risk is looking foolish.

That is why the hardest part of adult friendship is not finding people. It is finding people who will let a friendship begin slowly. A friendship that starts with a big dinner feels like an audition. A friendship that starts with a walk feels more survivable. You can talk, you can not talk, you can turn around and go home. A walk does not demand a performance. A walk says: we are here, we are not trapped, and if this is going to work, it can grow.

The best adult friendships I have seen often begin with something small and repeatable. Not a party, which is too diffuse. Not a date, which is too charged. Not a conference, which is too temporary. Something with a low threshold and a chance to happen again. A regular table at a bar, a walking route, a class where the same faces return, a volunteer shift where you are responsible for a small piece of the work. The activity gives the relationship a reason to exist before the relationship has earned the right to exist.

But even that is not enough. The person still has to choose the friendship. The activity can bring two bodies together, but it cannot make them care. Caring is the private part. It means noticing that the other person exists as more than a function. It means remembering a detail, asking a follow-up question, making the next plan before the first one has fully cooled. It means tolerating the fact that the other person is strange, or tired, or inconsistent, and deciding that the relationship is worth the trouble.

This is what school never taught. It gave us the room, but it did not teach us how to keep the room after we left it. It did not teach us how to be the person who says, “I would like to see you again, specifically, on a night when we are not required to be in the same place.” It did not teach us how to bear the silence of a friendship that has not yet proved itself.

So adult friendship is hard because it is late, chosen, and unguaranteed. It happens after we have learned enough to be cautious. It happens in lives that are full of obligations. It happens between people who cannot simply be placed next to each other and left. It requires a structure that no one provides, and it requires the courage to build it without knowing whether the other person will help.

That is not a reason to stop trying. It is a reason to try in the right way. Not by announcing a friendship, but by creating a small occasion for one. Not by demanding intensity, but by making repetition possible. Not by hoping the other person will notice, but by giving them a clear, low-cost way to say yes.

The adult friend is not the person you meet once and instantly like. The adult friend is the person you meet, and then meet again, and then make a plan with, and then keep. The friendship is not a spark. It is a habit that has not yet been born.

prompt: Is nostalgia actually about the past, or is it about the person we were then? Something essayistic, not a psych textbook summary.
response:
Nostalgia is a lie we tell ourselves to make the past bearable, and the lie works because it is about us, not then.

The past did not feel the way we remember it feeling. It had no soundtrack, no soft focus, no sense of being a chapter with a title. It had traffic, boredom, an ache in the knee, a Tuesday afternoon that went nowhere. What nostalgia actually reaches for is the version of you who was in that past: younger, less burdened, more certain, loved in ways you no longer receive, or at least loved in ways you no longer have to defend. The past is the stage; the person is the audience’s reason for staying.

That is why nostalgia is so often aimed at moments that were not especially good. The first car, the kitchen table, the summer before leaving, the last year of school. These are not always the happiest times. They are the times when you still had the problem of being alive in a form that had not yet been solved. You were in the middle of your life, which is the only position from which it can look like a life. Now you are in the aftermath. The past is not remembered for its texture so much as for the fact that you were still inside it, still allowed to be surprised by it.

There is also a selfishness in nostalgia that we do not usually admit. To be nostalgic for a time is to be nostalgic for a time in which you had not yet become fully responsible for who you have become. The person you were then had not yet made all the choices you have made since, had not yet seen the consequences of some of them, had not yet had to live inside the self you now have to wear. Nostalgia is the desire to be forgiven in advance, or to return to a moment before the bill arrived.

This is why nostalgia can be so cruel. It can make the present feel like a betrayal. The present is where you have to be a specific adult in a specific body with specific debts and specific tastes. The past, by contrast, is a person you can still be proud of from a distance. You can love that person without having to be him or her again. You can keep him or her warm the way you keep a photograph warm: by not letting it into the room.

But the person you were then was also a person. Not a symbol. Not a state of innocence. He or she had bad habits, small vanities, cruelties, mistakes. Nostalgia smooths this out. It turns a human being into a condition. And that is the real error: not that the past was better, but that the past was a version of you that had not yet been tested by everything you now know.

The best defense against nostalgia is not to force yourself to be cheerful. It is to remember that the person you were then did not have the whole story. He or she was in the middle of it, which is why the moment looked so full of air. The air was not in the moment. It was in the fact that you did not know what would come next.

prompt: I'm a couples therapist (18 years). The single most predictive thing I see isn't conflict style, it's whether partners are curious about each other after the first decade. I'd like a short essay for my practice's blog developing that idea for a general audience. Warm but not saccharine. 700-900 words.
response:
# The Question You Should Keep Asking

In my first few years of practice, I assumed the hard marriages were the ones that fought. I imagined couples in the room with shoulders up around their ears, one talking over the other, a long silence where the real damage had been done. I expected the easy marriages to be the calm ones, the ones who could name a few problems and then move on to lighter things.

What I keep finding is that neither of those pictures is the real dividing line.

The difference I see most often is quieter. It is whether, after many years together, each person still wants to know what the other is thinking and feeling.
